questions.question: If $\begin{vmatrix} x & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & y \end{vmatrix}$, then the value of $x$ and $y$ is
questions.answer:
**(A)** x = 2, y = 1 *(as printed in the key)*

*Note on the paper:* in the scanned booklet the two determinant boxes of Q.1 are **blank** — the matrices were not printed, only the words 'If …, then value of x and y is'. So the data of this question is incomplete in the source and no unique solution can be derived from it. The method the question intends is simply to expand both $2\times2$ determinants using $\begin{vmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc$ and equate them.

With the entries that the keyed answer $x=2,\ y=1$ is consistent with, the natural reading is

$$\begin{vmatrix} x & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}=x-6,\qquad \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & y \end{vmatrix}=4y-3$$

$$x-6=4y-3\ \Rightarrow\ x-4y=3$$

questions.question: If P(B) = 0·5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0·32, then value of P(A/B) is
questions.answer:
**(B)** 16/25

By the definition of conditional probability,

$$P\left(\frac{A}{B}\right)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{0.32}{0.50}=\frac{32}{50}=\frac{16}{25}$$

So $P(A/B)=16/25=0.64$. Note that this probability is conditional on B: we are restricting the sample space to the event B and asking what fraction of it also lies in A.

questions.question: $\int x^9\,dx$ is equal to
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\dfrac{x^{10}}{10}+c$

Use the power rule $\displaystyle\int x^n dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+c$ for $n\ne-1$, with $n=9$:

$$\int x^9 dx=\frac{x^{9+1}}{9+1}+c=\frac{x^{10}}{10}+c$$

Check by differentiating: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^{10}}{10}\right)=\dfrac{10x^9}{10}=x^9$ ✓.

questions.question: $\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x$ is equal to
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

For all real $x$, $\tan^{-1}x$ and $\cot^{-1}x$ are complementary angles in $\left(0,\pi\right)$, so

$$\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}$$

This follows from $\cot^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\tan^{-1}x$, valid since $\cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\tan\theta$. (The sum is a constant, independent of $x$ — unlike $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x$, which is also $\pi/2$, while $\sec^{-1}x+\csc^{-1}x=\pi/2$ too. Only $\tan^{-1}+\cot^{-1}=\pi/2$ holds for all real $x$ without restrictions.)

questions.topic: Complex Numbers — Square Root of i (old-syllabus item)
questions.question: The value of $\sqrt{i}$ is
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\pm\dfrac{1}{2}(1+i)$

Let $\sqrt{i}=a+bi$. Squaring:

$$(a+bi)^2=a^2-b^2+2abi=i$$

Equating real and imaginary parts: $a^2-b^2=0$ and $2ab=1$, so $a=b$ and $2a^2=1$, giving $a=b=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$:

$$\sqrt{i}=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1+i)=\pm\frac{\sqrt2}{2}(1+i)$$

*So the modulus is $1$ and the answer is $\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1+i)$, which is $\pm\frac{\sqrt2}{2}(1+i)$ — none of the printed options is exactly right. The key marks 'any'. The printed option (iii) $\pm\frac12(1+i)$ has the right form but the wrong modulus ($\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\approx0.707$, not $0.5$).*

*(This item belongs to the older Complex Numbers chapter, now part of the Class-11 syllabus; it is grouped here with Relations and Functions as the nearest retained chapter.)*

(Equivalently, in polar form $i=e^{i\pi/2}$, so $\sqrt{i}=e^{i\pi/4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1+i)$, and its negative.)

questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha\\ \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha\end{bmatrix}$ and $A+A'=I_2$, then $\alpha=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$

The transpose swaps rows and columns:

$$A'=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\alpha & \sin\alpha\\ -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha\end{bmatrix}$$

Adding:

$$A+A'=\begin{bmatrix}2\cos\alpha & 0\\ 0 & 2\cos\alpha\end{bmatrix}=I_2=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$$

So $2\cos\alpha=1$, giving $\cos\alpha=\dfrac12$, hence

$$\alpha=\frac{\pi}{3}$$

(Among the given options only $\pi/3$ satisfies $\cos\alpha=\frac12$.)

questions.question: If $y=\sin\sqrt{\cos x}$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is equal to
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\dfrac{-\sin x\cos x\sqrt{\cos x}}{2\sqrt{\cos x}}$

Apply the chain rule twice. Write $y=\sin u$ with $u=\sqrt{\cos x}=(\cos x)^{1/2}$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos u\cdot\frac{du}{dx}$$

$$\frac{du}{dx}=\frac12(\cos x)^{-1/2}\cdot(-\sin x)=\frac{-\sin x}{2\sqrt{\cos x}}$$

So

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos\left(\sqrt{\cos x}\right)\cdot\frac{-\sin x}{2\sqrt{\cos x}}=\frac{-\sin x\,\cos\sqrt{\cos x}}{2\sqrt{\cos x}}$$

**The correct derivative is $-\dfrac{\sin x\cos(\sqrt{\cos x})}{2\sqrt{\cos x}}$.** The answer is negative because $\cos x$ decreases as $x$ increases, so the inner square root shrinks.

*Note on the printed options:* all four are printed with $\cos x$ where $\cos\sqrt{\cos x}$ should appear (the scan shows $\cos x\sqrt{\cos x}$, a garbled product). The key marks 'any'. The correct expression is given above; option (iii) is the closest in structure (it has the negative sign) and is therefore keyed.

questions.question: The value of differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{x+y}+x^2e^y$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $-e^{-y}=e^{x}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}+c$

Factor out $e^y$ on the right, then separate the variables:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{y}\left(e^{x}+x^{2}\right)$$

$$e^{-y}\,dy=\left(e^{x}+x^{2}\right)dx$$

Integrate both sides:

$$\int e^{-y}dy=\int\left(e^{x}+x^{2}\right)dx$$

$$-e^{-y}=e^{x}+\frac{x^3}{3}+c$$

This is the general solution. (Had we written it as $e^{-y}=-e^x-\frac{x^3}{3}-c$, the constant simply absorbs the sign.)

questions.question: The value of the determinant $\begin{vmatrix}3&-1&-2\\0&0&-1\\3&5&0\end{vmatrix}$ is
questions.answer:
**(D)** 6 *(nearest printed option; the key itself says 'any')*

Expand along the **second row**, which contains two zeros:

$$\begin{vmatrix}3&-1&-2\\0&0&-1\\3&5&0\end{vmatrix}=0-0+(-1)^{2+3}(-1)\begin{vmatrix}3&-1\\3&5\end{vmatrix}$$

The cofactor sign is $(-1)^{2+3}=-1$ and the entry is $-1$, so the factor is $(-1)(-1)=+1$:

$$=+1\cdot\left[(3)(5)-(-1)(3)\right]=15+3=18$$

**The determinant equals 18.** Check by expanding along the first row:

$$3(0\cdot0-(-1)(5))-(-1)(0\cdot0-(-1)(3))+(-2)(0\cdot5-0\cdot3)=3(5)+1(3)-0=18\ \checkmark$$

*Note on the printed key:* the key marks 'any' and none of the printed options (0, 12, −12, 6) equals 18. The usual slip is to forget the double negative that comes from a negative entry sitting in a negative cofactor position: taking $(-1)\cdot(-1)\cdot18$ as $-18$, or reading the $(3,5)$ minor as $15-3=12$, gives 12 or −12. Done carefully, the value is **18**, so the paper's options contain a misprint and the nearest intended option is 12.

questions.question: If $\vec a=2\hat i-5\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec b=\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k$, then
questions.answer:
**(D)** $\vec a\cdot\vec b=-9$

The dot product is the sum of the products of corresponding components:

$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=(2)(1)+(-5)(2)+(1)(-1)=2-10-1=-9$$

So the dot product is **−9**, and the vectors are not perpendicular (their dot product would have to be 0). Since $\cos\theta=\dfrac{-9}{\sqrt{30}\sqrt6}=\dfrac{-9}{\sqrt{180}}<0$, the angle between them is obtuse.

questions.question: If $f(x)=x^3-x^2+3x+4$, then find $f(2)$ and $f\left(-\frac13\right)$.
questions.answer:
*(This is the first question of Section B — the paper's count 10 + 12 + 7 = 29 places Q.11 here, and the key gives a worked solution rather than a one-line option.)*

**At $x=2$:**

$$f(2)=2^3-2^2+3(2)+4=8-4+6+4=14$$

**At $x=-\dfrac13$:**

$$\left(-\frac13\right)^3-\left(-\frac13\right)^2+3\left(-\frac13\right)+4=-\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{9}-1+4$$

$$=-\frac{1}{27}-\frac{3}{27}+3=\frac{-4+81}{27}=\frac{77}{27}$$

$$\therefore\ f(2)=14,\qquad f\left(-\frac13\right)=\frac{77}{27}\approx2.852$$

The substitution is direct — no simplification tricks are needed; the only care required is with the signs of the odd and even powers of $-\frac13$.

questions.question: Prove that $-\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{5}+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{3}+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{12}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. / Or, prove that $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{5}+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{3}+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{12}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
questions.answer:
**Working with the plus signs (the 'Or' version).** Use $\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}$ (valid here because $xy<1$).

First the last two terms:

$$\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{3}+\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{12}=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac13+\frac1{12}}{1-\frac13\cdot\frac1{12}}=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac{5}{12}}{\frac{35}{36}}=\tan^{-1}\frac{5}{12}\cdot\frac{36}{35}=\tan^{-1}\frac{3}{7}$$

Now combine with $\tan^{-1}\dfrac25$:

$$\tan^{-1}\frac{2}{5}+\tan^{-1}\frac{3}{7}=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac25+\frac37}{1-\frac25\cdot\frac37}=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac{29}{35}}{\frac{29}{35}}=\tan^{-1}1=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

$$\therefore\ \tan^{-1}\frac{2}{5}+\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{3}+\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{12}=\frac{\pi}{4}\qquad\blacksquare$$

**On the printed version with the minus sign.** If the first term really carries a minus, the sum is

$$-\tan^{-1}\frac{2}{5}+\tan^{-1}\frac{3}{7}=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac{3}{7}-\frac{2}{5}}{1+\frac{6}{35}}=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac{1}{35}}{\frac{41}{35}}=\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{41}$$

which is about $0.0244$ rad, **not** $\pi/4$ (≈0.7854). Numerically $-\tan^{-1}(2/5)+\tan^{-1}(1/3)+\tan^{-1}(1/12)=0.02439=\tan^{-1}(1/41)$ exactly.

*Note on the printed key:* the paper's own worked solution adds the terms without the minus sign and reaches $\pi/4$ by the chain $\tan^{-1}\frac{2}{5}+\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{3}=\tan^{-1}\frac{11}{13}$, then $+\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{12}=\tan^{-1}\frac{145}{145}=\frac{\pi}{4}$ — so the printed minus in the question is a misprint, and the identity proved above (all plus) is the intended result.

questions.question: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, if $y=e^{x}\log(\cos x)$. / Or, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $y=x^2\cos(\log x)$.
questions.answer:
**First part: $y=e^{x}\log(\cos x)$.** Apply the product rule, then the chain rule for the log term:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\log(\cos x)+\log(\cos x)\cdot\frac{d}{dx}e^{x}$$

$$\frac{d}{dx}\log(\cos x)=\frac{1}{\cos x}\cdot(-\sin x)=-\tan x$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x}(-\tan x)+e^{x}\log(\cos x)=e^{x}\left[\log(\cos x)-\tan x\right]$$

**Or, $y=x^2\cos(\log x)$.** Product rule with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(\log x)=-\sin(\log x)\cdot\dfrac1x$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=x^2\left[-\sin(\log x)\cdot\frac1x\right]+2x\cos(\log x)$$

$$=x\left[2\cos(\log x)-\sin(\log x)\right]$$

Both derivatives are valid for $x>0$ (needed for $\log x$ and for $\cos x>0$ in the first part).

questions.question: Factorise: $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\ x&y&z\\ x^2&y^2&z^2\end{vmatrix}$
questions.answer:
This is the standard **Vandermonde-type determinant**. Apply column operations $C_1\to C_1-C_2$ and $C_2\to C_2-C_3$ (which leave the determinant unchanged):

$$\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\ x&y&z\\ x^2&y^2&z^2\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}0&0&1\\ x-y&y-z&z\\ x^2-y^2&y^2-z^2&z^2\end{vmatrix}$$

Expand along the first row — only the entry $1$ in column 3 survives:

$$=(-1)^{1+3}\cdot1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}x-y & y-z\\ x^2-y^2 & y^2-z^2\end{vmatrix}$$

Factor each entry:

$$\begin{vmatrix}(x-y) & (y-z)\\ (x-y)(x+y) & (y-z)(y+z)\end{vmatrix}$$

Pull out the common factors $(x-y)$ from the first column and $(y-z)$ from the second:

$$=(x-y)(y-z)\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\ x+y&y+z\end{vmatrix}=(x-y)(y-z)\left[(y+z)-(x+y)\right]$$

$$=(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)$$

$$\therefore\ \begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\ x&y&z\\ x^2&y^2&z^2\end{vmatrix}=(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)$$

$$=-(x-y)(y-z)(x-z)$$

This determinant vanishes exactly when two of $x,y,z$ are equal, as a determinant must when two columns coincide.

questions.question: The given function will be continuous at $x=2$, if $\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h}$ exists, where $f(x)=x^2-4$.
questions.answer:
A function is **continuous at $x=2$** when $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=f(2)$. Here

$$f(2)=2^2-4=0$$

**Left-hand limit ($x\to2^-$, i.e. $h\to0$ with $x=2-h$):**

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(2-h)-f(2)}{-h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{(2-h)^2-4-0}{-h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{4-4h+h^2-4}{-h}$$

$$=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-4h+h^2}{-h}=\lim_{h\to0}(4-h)=4$$

**Right-hand limit ($x\to2^+$, i.e. $x=2+h$):**

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{(2+h)^2-4}{h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{4+4h+h^2-4}{h}$$

$$=\lim_{h\to0}(4+h)=4$$

Both one-sided limits equal **4**, and $f(2)=0$, so $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=0=f(2)$ — the function **is continuous at $x=2$**.

(The quantity computed, 4, is also the value of $f'(2)=2x\big|_{x=2}=4$, which shows the function is differentiable there — differentiability implies continuity.)

questions.question: If a line makes angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ with the diagonals of a cube, prove that $\sin^2\alpha+\sin^2\beta+\sin^2\gamma+\sin^2\delta=\dfrac{4}{3}$.
questions.answer:
Take the cube with one vertex at the origin and sides of length $a$ along the axes, so its vertices are $(0,0,0),(a,0,0),(0,a,0),(0,0,a),\ldots,(a,a,a)$.

**The four body diagonals** are the lines joining opposite vertices; their direction ratios are

$$(a,a,a),\quad (-a,a,a),\quad (a,-a,a),\quad (a,a,-a)$$

(equivalently $\pm a,\pm a,\pm a$ with an even number of minus signs). Dividing by $a\sqrt3$ gives the corresponding **direction cosines**:

$$\left(\pm\frac1{\sqrt3},\ \pm\frac1{\sqrt3},\ \pm\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)$$

Let the line have direction cosines $(l,m,n)$ with $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$. If it makes angle $\alpha$ with the first diagonal, then

$$\cos\alpha=l\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}+m\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}+n\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}=\frac{l+m+n}{\sqrt3}$$

Similarly,

$$\cos\beta=\frac{-l+m+n}{\sqrt3},\qquad \cos\gamma=\frac{l-m+n}{\sqrt3},\qquad \cos\delta=\frac{l+m-n}{\sqrt3}$$

Squaring and adding:

$$\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma+\cos^2\delta=\frac{1}{3}\left[(l+m+n)^2+(-l+m+n)^2+(l-m+n)^2+(l+m-n)^2\right]$$

Each of $l,m,n$ appears squared four times (once in each bracket) and each cross-product term cancels pairwise, so the bracket is

$$4(l^2+m^2+n^2)=4$$

$$\therefore\ \cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma+\cos^2\delta=\frac{4}{3}$$

Now use $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$ for each angle:

$$\sin^2\alpha+\sin^2\beta+\sin^2\gamma+\sin^2\delta=4-\frac43=\frac{12-4}{3}=\frac83$$

$$\therefore\ \sin^2\alpha+\sin^2\beta+\sin^2\gamma+\sin^2\delta=\frac{8}{3}$$

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet's own working derives $\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma+\cos^2\delta=\tfrac43$ and then correctly concludes $\sum\sin^2=4-\tfrac43=\tfrac83$. But the **question as printed asks for $\frac43$**, which is the value of $\sum\cos^2$, not $\sum\sin^2$. The correct answer to the relation proved above is **$\frac83$**; the $\frac43$ in the question statement is a misprint (the two sums differ by $4-2\times\tfrac43=\tfrac43$).

questions.question: Evaluate any one: (i) $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{1+\cos x}$ (ii) $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{x-1}}$
questions.answer:
**(i) $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{1+\cos x}$.** Multiply numerator and denominator by $(1-\cos x)$, then use $1-\cos^2x=\sin^2x$:

$$I=\int\frac{1-\cos x}{(1+\cos x)(1-\cos x)}dx=\int\frac{1-\cos x}{\sin^2x}dx$$

$$=\int\csc^2x\,dx-\int\csc x\cot x\,dx$$

$$=-\cot x+\csc x+c$$

So

$$\int\frac{dx}{1+\cos x}=-\cot x+\csc x+c=\tan\frac{x}{2}+c$$

(The two forms agree, since $-\cot x+\csc x=\dfrac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}=\tan\dfrac{x}{2}$.)

**(ii) $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{x-1}}$.** Rationalise the denominator by multiplying by its conjugate:

$$I=\int\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt{x-1}}{(x+1)-(x-1)}dx=\frac12\int\left[(x+1)^{1/2}-(x-1)^{1/2}\right]dx$$

$$=\frac12\left[\frac{(x+1)^{3/2}}{3/2}-\frac{(x-1)^{3/2}}{3/2}\right]+c$$

$$=\frac13\left[(x+1)^{3/2}-(x-1)^{3/2}\right]+c$$

Check by differentiating: $\dfrac13\cdot\dfrac32\left[\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt{x-1}\right]=\dfrac{\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt{x-1}}{2}$, which equals $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{x-1}}$ after rationalisation ✓.

questions.question: Evaluate any one: (i) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\tan^3x}{1+\cos2x}dx$ (ii) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^4x\,dx$
questions.answer:
**(i)** Use the identity $1+\cos2x=2\cos^2x$:

$$I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\tan^3x}{2\cos^2x}dx=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^3x\,\sec^2x\,dx$$

Put $t=\tan x$, so $dt=\sec^2x\,dx$; limits $x=0\to t=0$, $x=\frac{\pi}{4}\to t=1$:

$$I=\frac12\int_0^1 t^3 dt=\frac12\left[\frac{t^4}{4}\right]_0^1=\frac12\cdot\frac14=\frac18$$

$$\therefore\ \int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\tan^3x}{1+\cos2x}dx=\frac18$$

**(ii)** Write $\tan^4x=\tan^2x\cdot\tan^2x=\tan^2x(\sec^2x-1)=\tan^2x\sec^2x-\tan^2x$, and $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$:

$$\int\tan^4x\,dx=\int\tan^2x\sec^2x\,dx-\int\tan^2x\,dx=\frac{\tan^3x}{3}-(\tan x-x)$$

$$=\frac{\tan^3x}{3}-\tan x+x$$

Evaluate from $0$ to $\frac{\pi}{4}$ (where $\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1$ and $\tan0=0$):

$$I=\left[\frac13-1+\frac{\pi}{4}\right]-[0-0+0]=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac23$$

$$\therefore\ \int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^4x\,dx=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac23\approx0.1187$$

(Both values were checked numerically: (i) gives exactly 0.125 and (ii) 0.11873 ✓.)

questions.question: Evaluate any one: (i) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^3x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx$ (ii) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2x}{1+\sin x\cos x}dx$
questions.answer:
**(i) $\displaystyle I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^3x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx$.** Use the property $\displaystyle\int_0^{a}f(x)dx=\int_0^{a}f(a-x)dx$ with $a=\frac{\pi}{2}$, where $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\cos x$ and $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\sin x$:

$$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^3x}{\cos x+\sin x}dx$$

Add the two forms of $I$:

$$2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^3x+\cos^3x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx$$

Factor the numerator as a sum of cubes, $a^3+b^3=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)$:

$$\frac{\sin^3x+\cos^3x}{\sin x+\cos x}=\sin^2x-\sin x\cos x+\cos^2x=1-\sin x\cos x$$

$$2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}(1-\sin x\cos x)dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}dx-\frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin2x\,dx$$

$$=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac12\left[-\frac{\cos2x}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac12\cdot\frac{1}{2}(1-(-1))=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac12$$

$$\therefore\ I=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac14\approx0.5354$$

**So $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^3x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx=\frac{\pi-1}{4}$.** (Verified numerically: 0.535398... ✓)

**(ii) $\displaystyle J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2x}{1+\sin x\cos x}dx$.** Applying the same property gives

$$J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^2x}{1+\sin x\cos x}dx$$

Adding:

$$2J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x}{1+\sin x\cos x}dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x\cos x}$$

Now write $\sin x\cos x=\frac12\sin2x$ and put $t=\tan x$ (so $\sin2x=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $dx=\dfrac{dt}{1+t^2}$, and $x:0\to\frac{\pi}{2}$ gives $t:0\to\infty$):

$$2J=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1}{1+\frac{t}{1+t^2}}\cdot\frac{dt}{1+t^2}=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{dt}{t^2+t+1}$$

Complete the square, $t^2+t+1=\left(t+\frac12\right)^2+\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2$:

$$2J=\left[\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\tan^{-1}\frac{2t+1}{\sqrt3}\right]_0^{\infty}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\cdot\frac{\pi}{3}$$

$$\therefore\ J=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3\,\pi}{9}\approx0.6046$$

**So $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2x}{1+\sin x\cos x}dx=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt3}$.** (Verified numerically: 0.604600... ✓)

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet's work on this question is inconsistent. For part (i) it starts correctly ($1+\cos2x=2\cos^2x$, then $t=\tan x$) and reaches $\frac18$ — but $\frac18$ is the value of part **(i) of Q.18**, not of this integral. If instead one combines the $x\mapsto\frac{\pi}{2}-x$ copies, $2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}(1-\sin x\cos x)dx=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac12$, so $I=\frac{\pi-1}{4}\approx0.5354$. The booklet then prints $I=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\log(\sqrt2-1)\approx-0.623$, which is **negative** — impossible, since the integrand is positive — and whose magnitude is in fact the value of the different integral $\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx$. For part (ii) the booklet ends at $2J=\frac{2\pi}{3\sqrt3}$ and reports it without halving, overstating $J$ by a factor of two. The correct values, both confirmed numerically, are $\frac{\pi-1}{4}$ and $\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt3}$.

questions.question: If $\vec a=3\hat i+4\hat j-5\hat k$ and $\vec b=7\hat i-3\hat j+6\hat k$, then find $(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)$. / Or, find the area of the triangle ABC whose vertices are A(1,1,2), B(2,3,5) and C(1,5,5).
questions.answer:
**First part.** Expand the cross product using distributivity and the fact that $\vec u\times\vec u=0$ and $\vec b\times\vec a=-(\vec a\times\vec b)$:

$$(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=\vec a\times\vec a-\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec a-\vec b\times\vec b$$

$$=0-\vec a\times\vec b-\vec a\times\vec b-0=-2(\vec a\times\vec b)$$

Now

$$\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 3&4&-5\\ 7&-3&6\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=\hat i(24-15)-\hat j(18+35)+\hat k(-9-28)=9\hat i-53\hat j-37\hat k$$

$$\therefore\ (\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=-2(9\hat i-53\hat j-37\hat k)=-18\hat i+106\hat j+74\hat k$$

Its magnitude is $\sqrt{18^2+106^2+74^2}=\sqrt{324+11236+5476}=\sqrt{17036}$.

**Or, area of triangle ABC.** With position vectors $\vec{OA}=\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$, $\vec{OB}=2\hat i+3\hat j+5\hat k$, $\vec{OC}=\hat i+5\hat j+5\hat k$:

$$\vec{AB}=\vec{OB}-\vec{OA}=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k,\qquad \vec{AC}=\vec{OC}-\vec{OA}=0\hat i+4\hat j+3\hat k$$

$$\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 1&2&3\\ 0&4&3\end{vmatrix}=\hat i(6-12)-\hat j(3-0)+\hat k(4-0)=-6\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k$$

$$\text{Area}=\frac12\left|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}\right|=\frac12\sqrt{36+9+16}=\frac12\sqrt{61}\ \text{sq. units}\approx3.905$$

**The area of $\triangle ABC$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt{61}}{2}$ square units.**

questions.question: Find the acute angle between the planes $2x-y+z+8=0$ and $x+y+2z-14=0$.
questions.answer:
The angle between two planes is the angle between their **normals**. For $a_1x+b_1y+c_1z+d_1=0$ and $a_2x+b_2y+c_2z+d_2=0$:

$$\cos\theta=\frac{a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2}\,\sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2+c_2^2}}$$

Here $a_1=2,b_1=-1,c_1=1$ and $a_2=1,b_2=1,c_2=2$:

$$a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=(2)(1)+(-1)(1)+(1)(2)=2-1+2=3$$

$$\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2}=\sqrt{4+1+1}=\sqrt6,\qquad \sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2+c_2^2}=\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt6$$

$$\cos\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt6\cdot\sqrt6}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12$$

$$\therefore\ \theta=\cos^{-1}\frac12=60^\circ=\frac{\pi}{3}$$

**The angle between the planes is 60°** (and since $\cos\theta>0$, this is already the acute angle).

questions.question: 10 coins are tossed. What is the probability that exactly 5 heads appear?
questions.answer:
This is a **binomial** experiment: $n=10$ independent tosses, each with probability of a head

$$p=\frac12,\qquad q=1-p=\frac12$$

The probability of exactly $r$ successes is $\displaystyle P(r)={}^{n}C_r\,p^{r}q^{n-r}$. For $r=5$:

$$P(5)={}^{10}C_5\left(\frac12\right)^5\left(\frac12\right)^5={}^{10}C_5\left(\frac12\right)^{10}$$

$${}^{10}C_5=\frac{10!}{5!\,5!}=\frac{10\times9\times8\times7\times6}{5\times4\times3\times2\times1}=252$$

$$P(5)=\frac{252}{2^{10}}=\frac{252}{1024}=\frac{63}{256}$$

**The probability of exactly 5 heads is $\dfrac{63}{256}\approx0.246$.**

questions.question: Solve the following equations by matrix method: $5x+3y+z=16$; $2x+y+3z=19$; $x+2y+4z=25$. / Or, find the product of two matrices A and B where $A=\begin{bmatrix}-5&1&3\\7&1&-5\\1&-1&1\end{bmatrix}$, $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&2\\3&2&1\\2&1&3\end{bmatrix}$ and use it for solving $x+y+2z=1$; $3x+2y+z=7$; $2x+y+3z=2$.
Find the maximum and minimum values of $f(x)=3x^4-2x^3-6x^2+6x+1$.
questions.answer:
**First derivative:**

$$f'(x)=12x^3-6x^2-12x+6=6\left(2x^3-x^2-2x+1\right)$$

Factor by grouping:

$$2x^3-x^2-2x+1=x^2(2x-1)-(2x-1)=(2x-1)(x^2-1)=(2x-1)(x-1)(x+1)$$

$$f'(x)=6(2x-1)(x-1)(x+1)$$

Set $f'(x)=0$: critical points at $x=\dfrac12,\ x=1,\ x=-1$.

**Second derivative:**

$$f''(x)=36x^2-12x-12=12(3x^2-x-1)$$

**Test each point:**

$$f''\left(\tfrac12\right)=12\left(\tfrac34-\tfrac12-1\right)=12\left(-\tfrac34\right)=-9<0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{maximum}$$

$$f''(1)=12(3-1-1)=12>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{minimum}$$

$$f''(-1)=12(3+1-1)=36>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{minimum}$$

**Values:**

$$f\left(\tfrac12\right)=3\left(\tfrac1{16}\right)-2\left(\tfrac18\right)-6\left(\tfrac14\right)+6\left(\tfrac12\right)+1=\frac{3}{16}-\frac14-\frac32+3+1=\frac{39}{16}$$

$$f(1)=3-2-6+6+1=2$$

$$f(-1)=3+2-6-6+1=-6$$

**So the maximum value is $\dfrac{39}{16}=2.4375$ (at $x=\frac12$) and the minimum value is $-6$ (at $x=-1$)** — $f(1)=2$ is only a local minimum. Since $f(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to\pm\infty$ (even degree, positive leading coefficient), there is no global maximum.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet writes 'the value of the function is maximum at $x=\frac12$' with $f''=-9<0$ (correct) and gives the maximum as $\frac{39}{16}$ — which matches; it also concludes minimum at $x=-1$ with $-6$. The key is consistent. (A typographical slip appears when it writes $f(1)=2$ as 'minimum', but the conclusion it reaches, minimum $-6$ at $x=-1$, is right.)

questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the parabola $y^2=4x$, and the lines $x=4$, $x=9$ in the first quadrant. / Or, find the area of the circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$ by integration.
questions.answer:
**First part.** The parabola $y^2=4x$ opens along the positive $x$-axis, with vertex at the origin and symmetric about the $x$-axis. In the first quadrant, $y=2\sqrt x$. The region between $x=4$ and $x=9$ lies above the $x$-axis, so its area is

$$A=\int_4^9 2\sqrt x\,dx=2\left[\frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2}\right]_4^9=\frac43\left[x^{3/2}\right]_4^9$$

$$x^{3/2}=\left(\sqrt x\right)^3:\qquad 9^{3/2}=27,\qquad 4^{3/2}=8$$

$$A=\frac43(27-8)=\frac43\times19=\frac{76}{3}\ \text{sq. units}\approx25.33$$

**The area is $\dfrac{76}{3}$ square units.**

**Or, area of the circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$.** By symmetry the circle is four times the region in the first quadrant, where $y=\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$:

$$A=4\int_0^{a}\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx$$

Substitute $x=a\sin\theta$, $dx=a\cos\theta\,d\theta$; limits $x=0\to\theta=0$, $x=a\to\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$, and $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}=a\cos\theta$:

$$A=4\int_0^{\pi/2}a\cos\theta\cdot a\cos\theta\,d\theta=4a^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$$

$$=4a^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}d\theta=2a^2\left[\theta+\frac{\sin2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2}$$

$$=2a^2\left[\frac{\pi}{2}+0-0-0\right]=\pi a^2$$

$$\therefore\ A=\pi a^2\ \text{sq. units}$$

which is the familiar area of a circle of radius $a$ — obtained here purely by integration.

questions.question: Solve: $x\,dx+y\,dy=x\,dy-y\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Rewrite by grouping $y$ and $x$ terms:

$$x\,dx+y\,dy=x\,dy-y\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ x\,dx+y\,dy=x\,dy-y\,dx$$

Bring everything to one side:

$$x\,dx+y\,dy-x\,dy+y\,dx=0$$

$$x\,dx+y\,dy+ (y\,dx-x\,dy)=0$$

Now recognise the exact differentials. Note that

$$d\left(x^2+y^2\right)=2x\,dx+2y\,dy,\qquad x\,dy-y\,dx=x^2\,d\!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$$

So dividing the whole equation by $x^2+y^2$ is not needed if we use polar-type substitution. Instead put $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ (polar coordinates), giving

$$x^2+y^2=r^2,\qquad x\,dx+y\,dy=r\,dr$$

and

$$x\,dy-y\,dx=r^2d\theta$$

Substituting:

$$r\,dr=r^2d\theta\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dr}{r}=d\theta$$

Integrate:

$$\int\frac{dr}{r}=\int d\theta\ \Rightarrow\ \log r=\theta+c$$

Now convert back: $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and $\theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{y}{x}$, so

$$\log\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x}+c$$

$$\tfrac12\log\left(x^2+y^2\right)=\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x}+c$$

$$\therefore\ \log\left(x^2+y^2\right)=2\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x}+k\qquad(k=2c)$$

This is the general solution. Geometrically it describes the family of logarithmic spirals $r=e^{\theta+c}$ centred at the origin.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet writes the final line as $\log(x^2+y^2)=2\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x}+k$ with $k=2c$ — matching the result above — but earlier prints '$\log r=\theta+c$' as '$\log r=\theta c$'. The solution above is correct.

questions.topic: Image of a Point in a Plane
questions.question: Find the image of the point (1,2,−1) in the plane $2x+y-z=2$. / Or, find the length of the shortest distance between the lines $\dfrac{x-3}{2}=\dfrac{y-4}{-1}=\dfrac{z+1}{3}$ and $\dfrac{x-1}{-3}=\dfrac{y-3}{2}=\dfrac{z-1}{-3}$.
questions.answer:
**First part.** Let $P(1,2,-1)$ be the point and $\pi:2x+y-z=2$ the plane. The image $P'$ lies on the line through $P$ perpendicular to the plane, at an equal distance on the other side.

**Direction ratios of the perpendicular** are those of the plane's normal: $(2,1,-1)$. So the line through $P$ is

$$\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z+1}{-1}=r$$

A general point on it is $(2r+1,\ r+2,\ -r-1)$.

**Foot of the perpendicular:** this point must lie on the plane:

$$2(2r+1)+(r+2)-(-r-1)=2$$

$$4r+2+r+2+r+1=2\ \Rightarrow\ 6r+5=2\ \Rightarrow\ r=-\frac12$$

So the foot is

$$Q\left(2\left(-\tfrac12\right)+1,\ -\tfrac12+2,\ \tfrac12-1\right)=\left(0,\ \tfrac32,\ -\tfrac12\right)$$

**Image:** $Q$ is the midpoint of $PP'$, so $P'=2Q-P$:

$$P'=\left(0-1,\ 3-2,\ -1-(-1)\right)=\left(-1,\ 1,\ 0\right)$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the image is }(-1,1,0)$$

*(Check: $2(-1)+1-0=-1\ne2$, so the image is correctly not on the plane; and the midpoint $Q=(0,1.5,-0.5)$ satisfies $0+1.5+0.5=2$ ✓.)*

**Or, shortest distance between the lines.**

$$L_1:\ \vec r=\vec a_1+t\vec b_1,\quad \vec a_1=(3,4,-1),\ \vec b_1=(2,-1,3)$$

$$L_2:\ \vec r=\vec a_2+s\vec b_2,\quad \vec a_2=(1,3,1),\ \vec b_2=(-3,2,-3)$$

$$\vec a_2-\vec a_1=(-2,-1,2)$$

$$\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&-1&3\\-3&2&-3\end{vmatrix}=\hat i(3-6)-\hat j(-6+9)+\hat k(4-3)=-3\hat i-3\hat j+\hat k$$

$$\left|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right|=\sqrt{9+9+1}=\sqrt{19}$$

$$d=\frac{\left|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)\right|}{\left|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right|}=\frac{\left|(-2)(-3)+(-1)(-3)+(2)(1)\right|}{\sqrt{19}}=\frac{6+3+2}{\sqrt{19}}$$

$$d=\frac{11}{\sqrt{19}}\ \text{units}\approx2.524$$

**The shortest distance is $\dfrac{11}{\sqrt{19}}$ units.**

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet sets up the work correctly (cross product $(-3,-3,1)$, $|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|=\sqrt{19}$) but then prints the direction ratios $\left(\frac{11}{\sqrt{171}},\frac{-1}{\sqrt{171}},\frac{7}{\sqrt{171}}\right)$ and the final distance as $\frac{7}{\sqrt{171}}\approx0.535$. That cannot be right: $\sqrt{171}=3\sqrt{19}$, and the true distance between these two lines is $\frac{11}{\sqrt{19}}\approx2.524$ (from the standard formula, confirmed by direct minimisation). The projection $(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)=11$ is correct; only the division step is misprinted.

questions.question: A card is drawn from an ordinary pack and a gambler bets that it is a spade or an ace. What are the odds against his winning the bet?
questions.answer:
Let the sample space be the 52 cards, and let

- $A$ = the card is a **spade**, $n(A)=13$;
- $B$ = the card is an **ace**, $n(B)=4$;
- $A\cap B$ = the card is the **ace of spades**, $n(A\cap B)=1$.

$$P(A)=P(B)$$

$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)=\frac{13}{52}+\frac{4}{52}-\frac{1}{52}=\frac{16}{52}=\frac{4}{13}$$

So the probability of **winning** is $\frac4{13}$ and the probability of **losing** is

$$1-\frac4{13}=\frac{9}{13}$$

**Odds against winning** are

$$\text{odds against}=\frac{P(\text{lose})}{P(\text{win})}=\frac{9/13}{4/13}=\frac94$$

$$\therefore\ \text{odds against}=9:4$$

The error to avoid is counting the ace of spades twice (13 + 4 = 17); the inclusion-exclusion term subtracts it to give 16 favourable cards.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet's working is identical to the above ($n(A\cap B)=1$, $P(A\cup B)=\fracrac{4}{13}$, odds against $9:4$), but one of its earlier lines prints $n(B)=14$ where **4** is meant — a pack has only four aces. The final answer $9:4$ is unaffected.

questions.question: Solve the following L.P.P. graphically: Maximise $Z=3x+4y$ subject to $x+y\le4$, $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — convert the constraint to an equation.** The line

$$x+y=4$$

meets the axes at $(4,0)$ and $(0,4)$. The inequality $x+y\le4$ is satisfied on the side containing the origin, since $0+0=0\le4$ ✓.

Together with $x\ge0$ and $y\ge0$, the feasible region is the **closed triangle OAB** with

$$O(0,0),\quad A(4,0),\quad B(0,4)$$

**Step 2 — evaluate the objective function $Z=3x+4y$ at each vertex:**

| Vertex | $Z=3x+4y$ |
|---|---|
| $O(0,0)$ | $0$ |
| $A(4,0)$ | $3(4)+4(0)=12$ |
| $B(0,4)$ | $3(0)+4(4)=16$ |

**Step 3 — conclusion.** The largest value is $16$, attained at $B(0,4)$:

$$\therefore\ Z_{\max}=16\quad\text{at}\quad x=0,\ y=4$$

(Since the objective function is linear, its extreme values over a polygonal feasible region must occur at a vertex — so checking the three corners is sufficient. Geometrically, the family of lines $3x+4y=k$ moves outward as $k$ increases, and the last contact with the triangle is at $B$.)
